metadata.title: A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting
metadata.venue: Journal of Computer and System Sciences, 55(1):119-139, 1997
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF (paper270.pdf) via Read tool's PDF rendering; the .txt fallback (paper270.txt) was severely garbled. Math fidelity should be high but cross-check against PDF if needed.

nodes.name: On-line allocation problem
nodes.statement: Allocator $A$ chooses distribution $\mathbf{p}^t$ over $N$ strategies on each trial $t=1,\ldots,T$, then receives loss vector $\boldsymbol{\ell}^t \in [0,1]^N$ from a (possibly adversarial) environment, suffering mixture loss $\mathbf{p}^t \cdot \boldsymbol{\ell}^t$.
nodes.statement_clean: Decide a distribution over $N$ strategies each round to minimize cumulative mixture loss against an adversary.

nodes.name: Cumulative loss and net loss
nodes.statement: $L_A = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbf{p}^t \cdot \boldsymbol{\ell}^t$ is the cumulative loss of $A$, $L_i = \sum_{t=1}^T \ell_i^t$ the cumulative loss of strategy $i$, and the goal is to minimize the net loss $L_A - \min_i L_i$.
nodes.statement_clean: Define the algorithm's cumulative loss, each strategy's cumulative loss, and the net loss to be minimized.

nodes.name: Hedge($\beta$)
nodes.statement: Multiplicative-weights algorithm for the on-line allocation problem: maintain weights $\mathbf{w}^t$, play $\mathbf{p}^t = \mathbf{w}^t / \sum_i w_i^t$, then update $w_i^{t+1} = w_i^t \, \beta^{\ell_i^t}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Multiplicative-weights on-line allocation algorithm parameterized by $\beta \in [0,1]$.
nodes.pseudocode: For $t = 1, 2, \ldots, T$: (1) choose allocation $\mathbf{p}^t = \mathbf{w}^t / \sum_{i=1}^N w_i^t$; (2) receive $\boldsymbol{\ell}^t \in [0,1]^N$; (3) suffer loss $\mathbf{p}^t \cdot \boldsymbol{\ell}^t$; (4) update $w_i^{t+1} = w_i^t \, \beta^{\ell_i^t}$.

nodes.name: General update rule $U_\beta$
nodes.statement: The analysis applies to any update of the form $w_i^{t+1} = w_i^t \cdot U_\beta(\ell_i^t)$ where $U_\beta : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ satisfies $\beta^r \le U_\beta(r) \le 1-(1-\beta)r$ for all $r \in [0,1]$.

nodes.name: Upper bound on $\sum_i w_i^{T+1}$ (Lemma 1)
nodes.statement: For any sequence of loss vectors $\boldsymbol{\ell}^1, \ldots, \boldsymbol{\ell}^T$, $\ln\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N w_i^{T+1}\right) \le -(1-\beta)\, L_{\mathbf{Hedge}(\beta)}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Use convexity bound $\alpha^r \le 1-(1-\alpha)r$ on each weight, multiply across $t=1,\ldots,T$, then apply $1+x \le e^x$.

nodes.name: Convexity inequality
nodes.statement: $\alpha^r \le 1 - (1-\alpha) r$ for $\alpha \ge 0$ and $r \in [0,1]$.

nodes.name: Per-step weight bound
nodes.statement: Combined with the update $w_i^{t+1} = w_i^t \beta^{\ell_i^t}$, $\sum_i w_i^{t+1} \le (\sum_i w_i^t)(1-(1-\beta)\mathbf{p}^t \cdot \boldsymbol{\ell}^t)$.

nodes.name: Telescope and exponentiate
nodes.statement: Iterate over $t$ and apply $1+x \le e^x$ to obtain $\sum_i w_i^{T+1} \le \exp(-(1-\beta) L_{\mathbf{Hedge}(\beta)})$.

nodes.name: Hedge net-loss bound (Theorem 2)
nodes.statement: For any sequence $\boldsymbol{\ell}^1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{\ell}^T$ and any $i \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$, $L_{\mathbf{Hedge}(\beta)} \le \frac{-\ln(w_i^1) - L_i \ln \beta}{1-\beta}$. More generally, for nonempty $S \subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$, $L_{\mathbf{Hedge}(\beta)} \le \frac{-\ln(\sum_{i \in S} w_i^1) - (\ln \beta)\, \max_{i \in S} L_i}{1-\beta}$.
conclusions: More generally $L_{\mathbf{Hedge}(\beta)} \le (-\ln(\sum_{i \in S} w_i^1) - (\ln \beta)\max_{i \in S} L_i)/(1-\beta)$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: From Equation (6) lower-bound $\sum_i w_i^{T+1} \ge \beta^{\max_{i \in S} L_i} \sum_{i \in S} w_i^1$, then combine with Lemma 1's upper bound.

nodes.name: Optimality of Hedge constants (Theorem 3)
nodes.statement: If algorithm $B$ for the on-line allocation problem satisfies $L_B \le c \min_i L_i + a \ln N$ for all $N, T$ and all loss sequences, then for every $\beta \in (0,1)$ either $c \ge \ln(1/\beta)/(1-\beta)$ or $a \ge 1/(1-\beta)$.
assumptions: $B$ is an on-line allocation algorithm with arbitrary number of strategies
There exist positive reals $a, c$ such that for any $N$ and any sequence $\boldsymbol{\ell}^1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{\ell}^T$: $L_B \le c \min_i L_i + a \ln N$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Define a decision problem on the $K$-simplex matching Vovk's framework, lower-bound Vovk's hardness function $c(\beta)$, then reduce on-line allocation to it.

nodes.name: Define decision problem on $K$-simplex
nodes.statement: Set $\Delta = S_K$ ($K$-dimensional simplex), $\Omega = \{\mathbf{e}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{e}_K\}$, $\lambda(\delta, \mathbf{e}_i) \doteq \delta \cdot \mathbf{e}_i = \delta_i$; verify Assumptions 1--4.

nodes.name: Lower bound Vovk's $c(\beta)$
nodes.statement: Take $\mathcal{D}$ uniform on $\{\mathbf{e}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{e}_K\}$; then $c(\beta) \ge \ln(1/\beta)/(-K \ln(1-(1-\beta)/K))$.

nodes.name: Reduce on-line allocation to constructed decision problem
nodes.statement: Map any on-line allocation algorithm $A$ to the constructed decision problem; Vovk's Theorem 13 then forces the claimed bounds on $c$ or $a$ as $K \to \infty$.

nodes.name: Vovk's $(c,a)$-boundedness characterization (Theorem 13)
nodes.statement: A decision problem (on compact $\Delta$ with finite $\lambda$) is $(c,a)$-bounded if and only if for all $\beta \in (0,1)$, $c \ge c(\beta)$ or $a \ge c(\beta)/\ln(1/\beta)$, where $c(\beta) = \sup_{\mathcal{D} \in \mathcal{S}} \inf_{\delta \in \Delta} \sup_{\omega \in \Omega} \lambda(\delta,\omega) / \log_\beta \sum_{\varepsilon \in \mathrm{dom}(\mathcal{D})} \beta^{\lambda(\varepsilon,\omega)} \mathcal{D}(\varepsilon)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Vovk 1995, A game of prediction with expert advice

nodes.name: Choosing $\beta$ via $g(z)$ (Lemma 4)
nodes.statement: Suppose $0 \le L \le \bar L$ and $0 < R \le \bar R$. Let $\beta = g(\bar L/\bar R)$ where $g(z) = 1/(1+\sqrt{2/z})$. Then $(-L \ln \beta + R)/(1-\beta) \le L + \sqrt{2 \bar L \bar R} + R$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Sketch: use $-\ln \beta \le (1-\beta^2)/(2\beta)$ for $\beta \in (0,1]$ and substitute $\beta = g(\bar L/\bar R)$.

nodes.name: Hedge regret bound from Lemma 4
nodes.statement: For $\beta = g(\bar L / \ln N)$, $L_{\mathbf{Hedge}(\beta)} \le \min_i L_i + \sqrt{2 \bar L \ln N} + \ln N$, equivalently average per-trial $\le \min_i L_i / T + \sqrt{2 \bar L \ln N}/T + \ln N / T = O(\sqrt{(\ln N)/T})$.

nodes.name: Hedge bound for prediction with experts (Theorem 5)
nodes.statement: For any loss function $\lambda$, any set of $N$ experts, and any sequence of outcomes, $\sum_{t=1}^T \Lambda(\mathcal{D}^t, \omega^t) \le \min_i \sum_{t=1}^T \Lambda(\mathcal{E}_i^t, \omega^t) + \sqrt{2 \bar L \ln N} + \ln N$, where $\bar L \le T$ is an assumed bound on the best expert's expected loss and $\beta = g(\bar L / \ln N)$.
assumptions: $N$ experts each producing distribution $\mathcal{E}_i^t$ on $\Delta$ at time $t$
Hedge($\beta$) used as in Section 3 with $\beta = g(\bar L / \ln N)$

nodes.name: $k$-ary prediction (Example 1)
nodes.statement: $\Delta = \Omega = \{1,\ldots,k\}$ with $\lambda(\delta,\omega) = 1$ if $\delta \ne \omega$ and $0$ otherwise; the expected number of mistakes of the learner exceeds that of the best expert by at most $O(\sqrt{T \ln N})$.

nodes.name: Repeated matrix games / rock-paper-scissors (Example 2)
nodes.statement: $\lambda$ encodes a fixed game matrix (e.g.\ rock-paper-scissors); against an adversary, the learner's average per-round loss converges to the best pure strategy's loss at rate $O(1/\sqrt{T \log |\Delta|})$.

nodes.name: Min-max value of repeated games (Example 3)
nodes.statement: When experts are pure strategies, Hedge($\beta$) achieves expected loss within $O(1/\sqrt{T \log |\Delta|})$ of the value of the game (von Neumann min-max), even against an adversary with full knowledge of game and algorithm.

nodes.name: Predicting points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ / convex losses (Example 4)
nodes.statement: $\Delta = \Omega = $ unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\lambda(\delta,\omega) = \|\delta - \omega\|$; predicting the weighted average $\delta^t = \sum_i p_i^t \varepsilon_i^t$ and using convexity $\|\delta^t - \omega^t\| \le \sum_i p_i^t \|\varepsilon_i^t - \omega^t\|$ gives explicit error bounds.

nodes.name: Convexity inequality on $\lambda$
nodes.statement: $\|(a \delta_1 + (1-a)\delta_2) - \omega\| \le a\|\delta_1 - \omega\| + (1-a)\|\delta_2 - \omega\|$ for any $a \in [0,1]$, $\omega \in \Omega$.

nodes.name: Boosting problem (binary)
nodes.statement: Given training set $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_N,y_N)$ drawn from $\mathcal{P}$ on $X \times \{0,1\}$ and a weak learner WeakLearn that returns hypotheses $h_t : X \to [0,1]$ with error $\epsilon_t < 1/2$, combine the $h_t$ into a single hypothesis $h_f$ with arbitrarily small error.

nodes.name: Strong / weak PAC-learning algorithm
nodes.statement: A strong PAC-learning algorithm outputs, given $\epsilon, \delta > 0$, with probability $1 - \delta$ a hypothesis with error $\le \epsilon$ in time polynomial in $1/\epsilon$, $1/\delta$. A weak PAC-learner satisfies the same conditions but only for $\epsilon \ge 1/2 - \gamma$ where $\gamma > 0$.

nodes.name: AdaBoost
nodes.statement: Adaptive boosting algorithm: at each round $t$ feed WeakLearn the distribution $\mathbf{p}^t = \mathbf{w}^t / \sum_i w_i^t$, set $\beta_t = \epsilon_t/(1-\epsilon_t)$, update $w_i^{t+1} = w_i^t \, \beta_t^{1 - |h_t(x_i) - y_i|}$, and output the weighted-majority hypothesis $h_f$.
nodes.statement_clean: Adaptive boosting algorithm that combines weak hypotheses by a weighted-majority vote with weights $\log(1/\beta_t)$.
nodes.pseudocode: Initialize $w_i^1 = D(i)$. For $t=1,\ldots,T$: (1) $\mathbf{p}^t = \mathbf{w}^t / \sum_i w_i^t$; (2) call WeakLearn with $\mathbf{p}^t$ to get $h_t : X \to [0,1]$; (3) $\epsilon_t = \sum_{i=1}^N p_i^t |h_t(x_i) - y_i|$; (4) $\beta_t = \epsilon_t/(1-\epsilon_t)$; (5) $w_i^{t+1} = w_i^t \, \beta_t^{1-|h_t(x_i)-y_i|}$.

nodes.name: AdaBoost training-error bound (Theorem 6)
nodes.statement: If WeakLearn called by AdaBoost generates hypotheses with errors $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_T$, then the error $\epsilon = \Pr_{i \sim D}[h_f(x_i) \ne y_i]$ of the final hypothesis output by AdaBoost is bounded by $\epsilon \le 2^T \prod_{t=1}^T \sqrt{\epsilon_t (1-\epsilon_t)}$. Equivalently $\epsilon \le \exp(-2 \sum_t \gamma_t^2)$ where $\epsilon_t = 1/2 - \gamma_t$.
assumptions: AdaBoost is run with WeakLearn that returns $h_t : X \to [0,1]$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement: Adapt Lemma 1 / Theorem 2: bound $\sum_i w_i^{T+1} \le \prod_t (1-(1-\epsilon_t)(1-\beta_t))$, lower-bound the same sum by $\epsilon \cdot (\prod_t \beta_t)^{1/2}$ on the misclassified instances, then minimize the resulting $\beta_t$ choice.

nodes.name: Per-step weight upper bound
nodes.statement: $\sum_i w_i^{t+1} \le (\sum_i w_i^t)(1-(1-\epsilon_t)(1-\beta_t))$, hence $\sum_i w_i^{T+1} \le \prod_{t=1}^T (1-(1-\epsilon_t)(1-\beta_t))$.

nodes.name: Lower bound sum on errors
nodes.statement: Final hypothesis errs on $i$ only if $\prod_t \beta_t^{-|h_t(x_i)-y_i|} \ge (\prod_t \beta_t)^{-1/2}$; sum these to get $\sum_i w_i^{T+1} \ge \epsilon \cdot (\prod_t \beta_t)^{1/2}$.

nodes.name: Optimize $\beta_t = \epsilon_t/(1-\epsilon_t)$
nodes.statement: Combining bounds gives $\epsilon \le \prod_t (1-(1-\epsilon_t)(1-\beta_t))/\sqrt{\beta_t}$; setting derivative to zero in each factor yields $\beta_t = \epsilon_t/(1-\epsilon_t)$ and Equation (14).

nodes.name: KL form of AdaBoost bound (Eq. 21--22)
nodes.statement: $\epsilon \le \prod_{t=1}^T \sqrt{1-4\gamma_t^2} = \exp(-\sum_t \mathrm{KL}(1/2 \,\|\, 1/2 - \gamma_t)) \le \exp(-2 \sum_t \gamma_t^2)$; in the uniform case $\epsilon_t = 1/2 - \gamma$, this becomes $\epsilon \le (1-4\gamma^2)^{T/2} \le \exp(-2 T \gamma^2)$.

nodes.name: Vapnik's VC generalization bound (Theorem 7)
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a class of binary functions on $X$ with VC-dimension $d$. For sample $S$ of $N$ i.i.d.\ examples and any $\delta > 0$, $\Pr[\exists h \in H : |\hat\epsilon(h) - \epsilon_g(h)| > 2 \sqrt{(d(\ln(2N/d)+1) + \ln(9/\delta))/N}] \le \delta$.
nodes.origin_citation: Vapnik 1982, Estimation of Dependences Based on Empirical Data, Theorem 6.7

nodes.name: VC-dimension of $\Theta_T(H)$ (Theorem 8)
nodes.statement: If $H$ has VC-dimension $d \ge 2$, then the class $\Theta_T(H)$ of linear thresholds of $T$ functions in $H$ has VC-dimension at most $2(d+1)(T+1) \log_2(e(T+1))$. Hence final AdaBoost hypotheses lie in a class with this VC bound.
assumptions: $H$ is a class of binary functions with VC-dimension $d \ge 2$
$\Theta_T(H) = \{ \theta(\sum_{t=1}^T a_t h_t - b) : b, a_t \in \mathbb{R}, h_t \in H\}$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8
nodes.statement: View $h_f$ as a two-layer feed-forward network and apply Baum and Haussler's result on the number of dichotomies realizable by such networks; bound the size of a shattered set.

nodes.name: Soft-threshold AdaBoost bound (Theorem 9)
nodes.statement: Let $r(x_i) = \sum_t (\log 1/\beta_t) h_t(x_i) / \sum_t \log 1/\beta_t$ and $h_f = F \circ r$ where $F : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ satisfies $F(1-r) = 1 - F(r)$ and $F(r) \le \tfrac{1}{2} (\prod_{t=1}^T \beta_t)^{1/2 - r}$. Then $\epsilon \le 2^{T-1} \prod_{t=1}^T \sqrt{\epsilon_t(1-\epsilon_t)}$ (i.e.\ Theorem 6's bound improved by a factor 2).
assumptions: $r(x_i)$ defined as the weighted average of $h_t(x_i)$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9
nodes.statement: Bound $\epsilon = \sum_i D(i) F(|r(x_i) - y_i|)$ using $F$'s assumed bound, then express the resulting product as the sum-of-weights estimate from the proof of Theorem 6.

nodes.name: Bayesian interpretation
nodes.statement: Under conditional independence of hypothesis errors given the label, the Bayes-optimal decision rule is identical to AdaBoost's combination rule (with $\epsilon_t = \Pr[h_t(x) \ne y]$).

nodes.name: AdaBoost.M1
nodes.statement: Direct extension of AdaBoost to multi-class labels $Y = \{1,\ldots,k\}$: weak learner returns $h_t : X \to Y$, indicator error $\epsilon_t = \sum_i p_i^t [\![h_t(x_i) \ne y_i]\!]$, and final hypothesis is $h_f(x) = \arg\max_{y \in Y} \sum_t (\log 1/\beta_t) [\![h_t(x) = y]\!]$.
nodes.pseudocode: Initialize $w_i^1 = D(i)$. For $t=1,\ldots,T$: (1) $\mathbf{p}^t = \mathbf{w}^t/\sum_i w_i^t$; (2) call WeakLearn to get $h_t : X \to Y$; (3) $\epsilon_t = \sum_i p_i^t [\![h_t(x_i) \ne y_i]\!]$ (if $\epsilon_t > 1/2$, set $T = t-1$ and abort); (4) $\beta_t = \epsilon_t/(1-\epsilon_t)$; (5) $w_i^{t+1} = w_i^t \, \beta_t^{1 - [\![h_t(x_i) \ne y_i]\!]}$.

nodes.name: AdaBoost.M1 error bound (Theorem 10)
nodes.statement: Suppose WeakLearn called by AdaBoost.M1 generates hypotheses with errors $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_T$, each $\epsilon_t \le 1/2$. Then $\epsilon = \Pr_{i \sim D}[h_f(x_i) \ne y_i] \le 2^T \prod_{t=1}^T \sqrt{\epsilon_t(1-\epsilon_t)}$.
assumptions: WeakLearn returns hypotheses $h_t : X \to Y$ with $\epsilon_t \le 1/2$ for all $t$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 10
nodes.statement: Reduce AdaBoost.M1 to AdaBoost: define an AdaBoost example $(\bar x_i, \bar y_i) = (i, 0)$ and $\bar h_t(i) = [\![h_t(x_i) \ne y_i]\!]$; show by induction that all internal quantities coincide, then apply Theorem 6.

nodes.name: Pseudo-loss
nodes.statement: For a weak hypothesis $h : X \times Y \to [0,1]$, training instance $i$, and label-weighting $q : \{1,\ldots,N\} \times Y \to [0,1]$ with $\sum_{y \ne y_i} q(i,y) = 1$, the pseudo-loss is $\mathrm{ploss}_q(h, i) \doteq \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - h(x_i, y_i) + \sum_{y \ne y_i} q(i,y) h(x_i, y))$.

nodes.name: AdaBoost.M2
nodes.statement: Multi-class boosting with vector-valued weak hypotheses $h_t : X \times Y \to [0,1]$ that minimize pseudo-loss $\epsilon_t$ instead of classification error; weights are kept per (instance, incorrect-label) pair $(i, y)$, and the final hypothesis is $h_f(x) = \arg\max_{y \in Y} \sum_t (\log 1/\beta_t) h_t(x, y)$.
nodes.pseudocode: Initialize $w_{i,y}^1 = D(i)/(k-1)$ for $y \in Y - \{y_i\}$. For $t=1,\ldots,T$: (1) $W_i^t = \sum_{y \ne y_i} w_{i,y}^t$, $q_t(i,y) = w_{i,y}^t/W_i^t$, $D_t(i) = W_i^t/\sum_i W_i^t$; (2) call WeakLearn with $D_t$ and $q_t$ to get $h_t : X \times Y \to [0,1]$; (3) $\epsilon_t = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_i D_t(i)(1 - h_t(x_i, y_i) + \sum_{y \ne y_i} q_t(i,y) h_t(x_i, y))$; (4) $\beta_t = \epsilon_t/(1-\epsilon_t)$; (5) $w_{i,y}^{t+1} = w_{i,y}^t \, \beta_t^{(1/2)(1 + h_t(x_i, y_i) - h_t(x_i, y))}$.

nodes.name: AdaBoost.M2 pseudo-loss bound (Theorem 11)
nodes.statement: Suppose WeakLearn called by AdaBoost.M2 generates hypotheses with pseudo-losses $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_T$. Then $\epsilon = \Pr_{i \sim D}[h_f(x_i) \ne y_i] \le (k-1) 2^T \prod_{t=1}^T \sqrt{\epsilon_t (1 - \epsilon_t)}$.
assumptions: WeakLearn returns $h_t : X \times Y \to [0,1]$ with pseudo-loss $\epsilon_t$ as in Step 3

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: Reduce AdaBoost.M2 to AdaBoost via examples indexed by pairs $(i,y)$ with $y \ne y_i$; define $\bar h_t(i,y) = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - h_t(x_i,y_i) + h_t(x_i,y))$, verify identity of internal variables, then apply Theorem 6.

nodes.name: Oblivious weak hypothesis (Example 5)
nodes.statement: An oblivious hypothesis $h(x,y) = h(y)$ depending only on the label can satisfy pseudo-loss $< 1/2$ even when no oblivious hypothesis with prediction error $< 1/2$ exists, illustrating that pseudo-loss is easier to minimize.

nodes.name: AdaBoost.R
nodes.statement: Boosting for regression ($Y = [0,1]$): maintains piecewise-linear weights $w_{i,y}^t$ over (instance, $y$-value) pairs; weak learner returns $h_t : X \to Y$; final hypothesis is the weighted median $h_f(x) = \inf\{y : \sum_{t : h_t(x) \le y} \log(1/\beta_t) \ge \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_t \log(1/\beta_t)\}$.
nodes.pseudocode: Initialize $w_{i,y}^1 = D(i)|y - y_i| / Z$ where $Z = \sum_i D(i) \int_0^1 |y - y_i| dy$. For $t = 1,\ldots,T$: (1) $\mathbf{p}^t = \mathbf{w}^t / \sum_i \int_0^1 w_{i,y}^t dy$; (2) call WeakLearn with $\mathbf{p}^t$ to get $h_t : X \to Y$; (3) $\epsilon_t = \sum_i |\int_{y_i}^{h_t(x_i)} p_{i,y}^t dy|$ (abort if $\epsilon_t > 1/2$); (4) $\beta_t = \epsilon_t/(1-\epsilon_t)$; (5) $w_{i,y}^{t+1} = w_{i,y}^t$ if $y_i \le y \le h_t(x_i)$ or $h_t(x_i) \le y \le y_i$, else $w_{i,y}^t \beta_t$.

nodes.name: AdaBoost.R MSE bound (Theorem 12)
nodes.statement: Suppose WeakLearn called by AdaBoost.R generates hypotheses with errors $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_T$ as in Figure 5. Then the mean squared error $\epsilon = \mathrm{E}_{i \sim D}[(h_f(x_i) - y_i)^2]$ of the final hypothesis is bounded by $\epsilon \le 2^T \prod_{t=1}^T \sqrt{\epsilon_t (1-\epsilon_t)}$.
assumptions: WeakLearn returns $h_t : X \to Y$ with error $\epsilon_t$ as in Step 3 of AdaBoost.R

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 12
nodes.statement: Map each $(x_i, y_i)$ to a continuum of binary AdaBoost examples $\bar y_{i,y} = [\![y \ge y_i]\!]$, define density $\bar D(i,y) = D(i)|y-y_i|/Z$; show binary error in the reduced space equals $1/(2Z)$ times MSE in the original, then apply Theorem 6.
